name: Underdetermination
statement: The evidence never quite forces one theory on us: rival theories can fit the same facts.
statementAccent: rival theories can fit the same facts
meaning: Underdetermination is the thesis that the available evidence is insufficient to determine which theory we should hold, because for any body of evidence more than one theory can be made compatible with it, so evidence alone does not uniquely fix theory choice. Philosophers distinguish two main forms. Holist underdetermination, closely tied to the Duhem-Quine thesis, arises because hypotheses are tested only in bundles with auxiliary assumptions: when an observation conflicts with a prediction, logic does not tell us which part of the bundle to reject, so we can always save a hypothesis by revising elsewhere. This form is deductive in character and concerns which belief to give up in the face of recalcitrant evidence. Contrastive underdetermination, the stronger form, concerns which of several rival theories to believe, and its most dramatic version is the empirical-equivalence thesis: for a given theory there may be rival theories that entail exactly the same observational consequences yet are logically incompatible with it, so that no possible observation could decide between them. Classic illustrations include the point, noted by Newton himself, that his mechanics makes the same predictions whether the universe is at absolute rest or moving uniformly, and the curve-fitting problem, that infinitely many curves pass through any finite set of data points. Underdetermination is a central argument against scientific realism.
mechanism: Underdetermination undercuts the idea that evidence, by itself, singles out one theory as the one to believe. In its holist form the mechanism is the Duhem-Quine point: because a hypothesis yields testable predictions only in conjunction with auxiliary assumptions, a clash between prediction and observation condemns only the whole conjunction, leaving it open, as a matter of logic, which member to blame; one can preserve any hypothesis by adjusting the auxiliaries, so the evidence does not determine a unique revision. In its contrastive form the mechanism is empirical equivalence: if two theories entail all and only the same observation statements, then every possible observation is equally compatible with both, and no experiment, however refined, could favor one over the other on purely empirical grounds. Newton saw that his physics could not distinguish a universe at rest from one in uniform motion, since both yield identical observable behavior, and the curve-fitting case shows that any finite dataset is fit by endlessly many incompatible functions. Because empirical evidence runs out before theory choice is settled, something beyond the evidence must break the tie. Anti-realists conclude that we are not entitled to believe one theory's account of unobservable reality over an empirically equivalent rival, a line developed in van Fraassen's constructive empiricism. Realists respond that the non-empirical virtues of theories, simplicity, scope, explanatory power, and unification, legitimately guide choice, and that empirically equivalent rivals are often contrived and parasitic rather than genuine alternatives.

examples.text: Newton noted his mechanics predicts the same observations whether the universe is at absolute rest or moving uniformly.
Infinitely many incompatible curves pass through any finite set of data points, so the data underdetermine the curve.
Because hypotheses are tested in bundles, a failed prediction does not say which assumption to reject, leaving choice open.

variants.name: Holist underdetermination
variants.text: The Duhem-Quine form: a recalcitrant observation does not tell us which member of a tested bundle to revise.

variants.name: Contrastive underdetermination
variants.text: The form concerning rival theories, whose strong version is that empirically equivalent theories cannot be told apart by evidence.

whyItMatters: Underdetermination is one of the central problems in the philosophy of science, because it strikes at the confidence that empirical evidence can settle what to believe about the world. If theories are underdetermined by the evidence, then the evidence alone cannot compel a unique choice, and something else, whether non-empirical virtues, convention, or social factors, must be doing part of the work. This has major consequences for the scientific realism debate: underdetermination, especially in its empirical-equivalence form, is a leading argument against realism, since if a theory has an empirically equivalent rival we seem to have no evidential grounds for believing its particular account of unobservable reality, a line that underwrites van Fraassen's anti-realist constructive empiricism, which asks only for empirical adequacy. Underdetermination also connects to the Duhem-Quine thesis, to the theory-ladenness of observation, and to sociological and feminist accounts that see values filling the gap the evidence leaves. Realists have replied vigorously, questioning whether genuine empirical equivalents exist and defending the truth-conduciveness of theoretical virtues.

working.text: observe that the evidence is compatible with more than one theory, so it does not fix a unique choice.
distinguish holist underdetermination, about which belief to revise, from contrastive underdetermination, about rival theories.
consider whether non-empirical virtues, or nothing at all, can legitimately decide between the rivals.

limits: Underdetermination is a genuine and important thesis, but its strength and reach are contested, especially in its strong contrastive form. Realists argue that many alleged empirically equivalent rivals are contrived, parasitic constructions, generated algorithmically from a theory rather than developed as serious alternatives, and so do not show that real science faces underdetermination. They add that empirical equivalence is hard to establish and is defeasible, since as auxiliary assumptions and the boundary of the observable expand, theories once thought to make identical predictions may come apart. Realists deny that evidential ties, where they exist, leave theory choice groundless: non-empirical virtues such as simplicity, scope, explanatory power, and being least ad hoc are widely taken to be legitimate, truth-conducive guides that break the tie, so underdetermination by observation alone does not entail that all choice is arbitrary. The holist form shows only that logic does not dictate which belief to revise, not that revision is unconstrained by good reasons.
misreadings: Underdetermination is not the claim that evidence is irrelevant to theory choice, only that evidence alone does not uniquely determine it. Its weak holist form, that logic does not say which assumption to revise, is far more secure than its strong form, that genuine empirically equivalent rivals always exist, which is contested. And underdetermination by observation does not entail that theory choice is arbitrary, since non-empirical virtues may legitimately decide, so treating underdetermination as making evidence useless, as always supplying real rival theories, or as proving choice groundless, misreads the thesis.
origin: The thesis, rooted in Duhem and Quine, that evidence does not uniquely determine theory choice, arising in a holist form about which belief to revise and a contrastive form about empirically equivalent rival theories; a central argument against scientific realism.
